lessons.title: What DeFi claims to replace
lessons.content:
# What DeFi claims to replace

**DeFi** is a nickname for programs on a public computer that try to do jobs a company usually does: swap one token for another, hold two inventories as a pool, and lend against collateral. The nickname is not a product. The program is the product.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say what DeFi claims to replace, what it does not delete, and why a slogan on a website is not the same object as bytecode on a named chain. This academy will not tell you to buy a token, enter a pool, or chase a percentage.

## A company is a help desk with a ledger

A **centralised exchange** is a company. Binance, used here as an example of a centralised exchange, not as a ranking, keeps an internal ledger. You log in. You hold an IOU until you withdraw. The company can freeze a withdrawal and run a help desk. That parenting has a cost.

DeFi’s useful claim is narrower than “banks are over.” For swap, pool, and lend, a program can sit on a public book and run the same rule for every caller. Nobody at a desk decides whether your swap is allowed. The function either succeeds or it reverts. You already met that machine in the Ethereum course: an EOA signs, a contract runs, gas is paid in the native coin.

The claim does not delete humans. Teams still write the programs. Websites still sit in front of them. Admin keys still exist on many contracts. If you hear “no one is in charge,” ask who can pause, mint, or pull liquidity.

## Swap, pool, and lend are three jobs

Name the jobs before the brands. A **swap** is a trade inside a program: you send token A, the program sends token B from an inventory it already holds. A **pool** is that inventory. Two or more token balances sit in a contract because liquidity providers deposited them. A **lend** is a program that takes collateral and lets a borrower take another asset, usually with a health rule that can liquidate. There is no loan officer. There is a function.

TABLE
Job a company used to do | DeFi object that claims the job | What is still a company around the edges
Match a buyer and a seller | A pool plus a router program | The website that draws the buttons
Hold both sides of a market | Token balances in a pool contract | The team that deployed it, and any admin key
Take a deposit and make a loan | Lending program with collateral math | Oracles, frontends, and liquidation bots
Keep your coins overnight | Self-custody at your EOA, or a protocol that holds them | Wallet-app vendors and device vendors
ENDTABLE

## Replace is not the same as disappear

If a program replaces a company for the matching step, you still need a screen. That screen can lie. Intermediate already taught you that a contract account is bytecode, not a person you can email. DeFi adds a second costume: a branded app that *says* it is the protocol.

You will meet **routers**, **factories**, and **pools** in later modules. Hold one correction now: **the protocol is the deployed code on a chain ID you can name.** Ethereum mainnet is chain ID 1. BNB Smart Chain is chain ID 56. Same-looking addresses. Different books. A “DeFi app” that does not name the chain is not naming the protocol.

Crystal Stones is a **BEP-20** token on BNB Smart Chain. The published contract to verify, never to pay, is `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`. It is not a pool, not a router, and not academy checkout. This Intermediate track is **$10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout** or a third-party payment processor.

## What the slogan hides on day one

Three hides, before any math. **Custody still happens.** During a swap, tokens sit in programs. After a supply into a lending market, a program holds the asset. **Permissions still happen.** An **approve** is a standing debit order on a token contract. The Ethereum course already named it. DeFi lives on approvals. **Failure still costs.** A reverted swap still burns native coin for gas.

**Worked scenario.** A learner opens a wallet app and a website that says “Decentralised Exchange — swap any token, no company.”

1. The learner names the chain in the wallet: chain ID 1 or chain ID 56, not “crypto.”
2. The learner asks which object will be called: a router, a pool, a token, or only a picture on a website.
3. The learner checks native coin for gas — ETH on Ethereum, BNB on BSC — before any token row.
4. The learner refuses to treat Crystal Stones’ verify-only contract as a swap destination or a tuition address.
5. The learner practices, if at all, with a size that can vanish without taking rent.

DIAGRAM
WHAT THE SLOGAN DRAWS          WHAT THE BOOK ACTUALLY HOLDS
+----------------------+       +---------------------------+
|  "no company" logo   |       |  EOA (your key)           |
|  big APY banner      |       |  token program (list)     |
|  a swap button       |       |  router program           |
+----------+-----------+       |  pool program (inventory) |
           |                   +---------------------------+
           v                                ^
   website (can be swapped)                 |
           +------ signed call -------------+
                   (this is the protocol)
ENDDIAGRAM

## Education is the brake, not the on-ramp

This course teaches you to see swap, pool, and lend as programs so a lie has fewer rooms. It will not rank protocols. It will not invent yield. Crystal Stones’ RWA story is **their claim to verify**. Wallet apps such as Trust Wallet and MetaMask — examples of wallet apps, not endorsements — are still the signing room.

NOTE
Academy rule: DeFi is a set of programs, not a personality and not a shopping aisle. If a sentence cannot name the chain, the contract, and the function, it is a slogan. Slogans do not pay gas and they do not return tokens.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You now have the claim in one sentence: programs that try to replace a company for swap, pool, and lend. The next lesson splits custody from protocol so “non-custodial” stops being a sticker.

## Say this out loud

- DeFi is programs on a public computer that claim the jobs of swap, pool, and lend.
- A company can still sit around the edges: websites, admin keys, wallet apps, oracles.
- The protocol is deployed bytecode on a named chain ID, not a logo.
- Crystal Stones’ contract is verify-only on BSC, not a pool and not checkout.
- This academy will not tell you to buy a token to “join DeFi.”

Next: custody versus protocol — who holds the tokens while the function runs.

lessons.title: Custody vs protocol
lessons.content:
# Custody vs protocol

**Custody** means who can move an asset without asking you again. A **protocol** is the deployed program. People glue those words together as “non-custodial protocol,” as if the sticker were a lock. The sticker is a claim. You test it by asking where the tokens sit after each function.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to split three rooms: tokens at your EOA, tokens inside a protocol, and IOUs at a company. You should also refuse the sentence “I still have them because I can see them in the app.” This academy will not tell you to deposit anywhere.

## Three rooms, named so you stop mixing them

**Room 1: your EOA.** The token contract’s storage has a row for your address. You sign a `transfer` or you sign an `approve`. Nobody else can move that row unless you already granted an allowance, or unless the token program itself has an admin mint/freeze function. Self-custody lives here — with the token-program caveats the Ethereum course already taught.

**Room 2: a protocol.** You called `deposit`, `supply`, `addLiquidity`, or a swap that parks value in a pool. The token row now belongs to the contract’s address, or the program issued you a receipt token. The program’s functions decide whether you can exit. “Non-custodial” here means: **no company help desk holds a matching IOU.** It does not mean the program cannot trap you.

**Room 3: a company ledger.** Binance, as an example of a centralised exchange, shows a number. That number is an IOU until you withdraw to an address you control. The company is the custodian. That is a different design, not a moral ranking.

TABLE
Where the tokens sit | Who can move them next | What “I can see them” means
Your EOA’s row in the token program | Your key, or any spender you approved | A wallet view of a token list
A pool or lending contract | The program’s functions, plus any admin role | A website view of a position
A centralised exchange IOU | The company’s ledger rules | An account screen, not a chain row
A website’s screenshot | Nobody on-chain; it is a picture | Marketing
ENDTABLE

## Non-custodial is a claim about the company, not about risk

When a DeFi page says **non-custodial**, the honest translation is: we are not holding an IOU for you in a corporate database. The program holds the assets under its own rules. If those rules include `pause`, `mint`, or `withdrawByOwner`, a human with a key still has custody-like power. You verify that on an explorer, not on a landing page.

A swap that completes in one transaction can still pass your tokens through a router and a pool. For a moment the inventory sits in the pool. After success, you should hold token B at your EOA (minus fees). If the function reverts, you should still hold token A, and you still paid gas. Module 3 treats the swap path. Today’s job is the custody map.

Lending is the loud case. Supplying USDT to a lending program is not a bank deposit. The program now has the USDT. You hold a receipt. Exit is a function. Liquidation is also a function. Module 4.

## Wallet apps are views, not vaults

Trust Wallet and MetaMask — examples of wallet apps, not endorsements — show you rows. They do not custody the protocol’s inventory. If a DeFi site says “your funds are in your wallet” while you are an LP, the accurate sentence is: **your receipt is in your wallet; the inventory is in the pool.** Mixing those sentences is how people get surprised when a pool is drained and the receipt still exists as a number.

Crystal Stones remains a BEP-20 token to verify at `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`. Seeing that ticker in a “DeFi dashboard” does not move custody into a mineral vault. The RWA story is **their claim to verify**. Academy checkout is still **$10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout**, not a deposit into a pool and not a send to that contract.

**Worked scenario.** A learner is about to tap Supply on a lending website.

1. The learner names the token and the chain — USDT on BSC is not USDT on Ethereum.
2. The learner asks: after this transaction, which address holds the USDT row in the token program?
3. The learner looks up that address on BscScan (chain 56) or Etherscan (chain 1) and confirms it is a contract, not an EOA.
4. The learner looks for an exit function name, not only a supply button.
5. The learner does not send tuition or “whitelist” funds to Crystal Stones’ verify-only contract.

DIAGRAM
BEFORE SUPPLY                    AFTER SUPPLY
+------------------+             +------------------+
| Your EOA         |             | Your EOA         |
| USDT row: 100    |             | USDT row: 0      |
| receipt: none    |             | receipt: 100     |
+------------------+             +------------------+
                                 +------------------+
                                 | Lending program  |
                                 | USDT row: 100    |
                                 | (program custody)|
                                 +------------------+
ENDDIAGRAM

## What this split is for in a failure

If a website disappears and the program still allows withdraw, that is protocol without the app. If the program pauses, the app cannot save you. If you approved a hostile spender, the tokens may still be in “your wallet” on the screen while a bot empties the row. Custody is not a feeling. It is who can call the next successful move.

NOTE
Academy rule: “non-custodial” does not mean “cannot be taken.” It means “no company IOU.” Protocol risk, admin keys, and allowances are still custody-shaped powers. Practice with amounts you can lose.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can now point at three rooms — EOA, protocol, company — and ask which one holds the asset after a tap. Next: the website is not the protocol, even when it uses the real name.

## Say this out loud

- Custody means who can move the asset without asking you again.
- A protocol can hold tokens under functions; that is not a bank deposit and not an exchange IOU.
- “Non-custodial” is a claim about a company ledger, not a promise that exit always works.
- A wallet app shows rows; it does not custody a pool’s inventory.
- Crystal Stones’ contract is verify-only; checkout is USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout.

Next: apps are not the protocol — the website can be swapped while the bytecode stays.

lessons.title: Apps are not the protocol
lessons.content:
# Apps are not the protocol

The **app** is a website or a mobile screen that draws buttons. The **protocol** is bytecode already sitting on a chain. Attackers prefer to swap the app because swapping the bytecode on a public computer is harder than cloning a page.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to separate frontend, wallet-connect session, router, and pool, and you should treat a familiar logo as a costume. This academy will not tell you which site to use. It will tell you what to name before you sign.

## Four layers people flatten into one button

**Frontend.** HTML, servers, domain names. Anyone who controls the domain or the script can change the spender address the wallet will be asked to approve. Bookmarks help. They do not make a domain immortal.

**Wallet connection.** The site asks a wallet app — Trust Wallet and MetaMask are examples — to share an address and later to sign. Connecting is not depositing. Connecting is handing the site a view of your address and a channel to *request* signatures. You can still refuse each request.

**Router.** A program that takes your swap (or add-liquidity) call and talks to pools. You often approve the router, not the pretty domain. Module 2 treats routers.

**Pool.** The inventory program. The router is a path. The pool is the shelf.

TABLE
Layer | Lives where | What a clone can fake | What a clone cannot fake without you
Frontend | A server and a domain | Logos, numbers, “verified” badges | Your private key, unless you type it
Wallet connect | A session in the wallet app | A request that looks like the real app | A signature you refuse
Router | A contract on a chain | A different router with a similar name | The original router’s bytecode
Pool | A contract holding tokens | A copycat pool with the same ticker letters | The original pool’s storage
ENDTABLE

## The real name on a fake page

A phishing site can print the real protocol name, the real Twitter handle, even the real contract hex in a footer, while the **Approve** request names a different spender. You do not verify the page’s footer. You verify the address in the wallet’s signature screen, then you verify that address on the explorer you typed from a bookmark: Etherscan for chain 1, BscScan for chain 56.

The Ethereum course already taught ABI and the idea that a wallet shows a function name if it knows the interface. “Contract interaction” without a named function is a stop sign until you understand the spender. Unlimited approve to an unknown spender is Module 6’s wound. Today’s wound is simpler: **the app is replaceable.**

Search ads, fake in-app browsers, and misspelled domains all attack this layer. Staff of this academy will never ask you to connect a wallet “so we can see your homework,” and will never ask for a seed phrase, a private key, or a 2FA code.

## What you actually sign

When the wallet pops, you are not signing “the website.” You are signing a transaction or a typed-data request that will hit a chain. Read: network (chain ID), spender or `to` address, token, amount or the word unlimited, and fee in the native coin. If the site said BSC and the wallet says Ethereum, you are already in a wrong-chain story. Module 6 treats that failure.

Crystal Stones’ published hex is for verification of a BEP-20 token, not for connecting a mystery dashboard. A site that says “official Crystal Stones DeFi, approve to farm” is selling a slogan. This academy does not run a farm. Tuition is **$10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout**.

**Worked scenario.** A learner types a protocol name into a search box and clicks the first result.

1. The learner does not connect yet. The learner checks the domain spelling against a source they already trust, not against the page’s own banner.
2. The learner opens the explorer from a bookmark and pastes the router address the docs named — if the page named none, that is a finding.
3. The learner connects the wallet only after the network in the wallet matches that explorer’s chain.
4. On the first signature request, the learner reads the spender hex and compares it to the explorer, character by character at start and end.
5. The learner rejects any request that asks for a seed, a screenshot of recovery words, or remote screen control.

DIAGRAM
SIDE BY SIDE
REAL STACK                         HOSTILE APP WITH REAL NAME
+-------------------+              +-------------------+
| website A         |              | website B (clone) |
| wallet connect    |              | wallet connect    |
+---------+---------+              +---------+---------+
          |                                  |
          v                                  v
+-------------------+              +-------------------+
| router 0xREAL...  |              | spender 0xBAD...  |
| pool 0xPOOL...    |              | drain program     |
+-------------------+              +-------------------+
Same logo. Different "to" address. The book will run either.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Disconnect is not revoke

Disconnecting a site in a wallet app stops new requests from that session. It does not set allowance to zero. Allowance lives in the token program’s storage. Module 2 will teach you to read it and to revoke it. Do not leave this lesson thinking the plug is the permission.

NOTE
Academy rule: a logo is not a checksum. The checksum is the chain ID plus the contract hex plus the function you are about to sign. If any of those three is only a picture, you do not sign.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can now point at the app as a replaceable costume and at the protocol as bytecode on a book. Next: BSC DeFi and Ethereum DeFi as the same family on two books.

## Say this out loud

- The app is a website. The protocol is deployed code on a chain.
- Connecting a wallet is a session, not a deposit and not an approval.
- A fake frontend can print a real contract name and still ask you to approve a different spender.
- Disconnect is not revoke; allowance lives in the token program.
- Academy staff never ask for a seed, a key, or 2FA codes to “connect DeFi.”

Next: same family of programs on Ethereum and on BNB Smart Chain — two books, not two nicknames.

lessons.title: BSC DeFi vs Ethereum DeFi (same family, different book)
lessons.content:
# BSC DeFi vs Ethereum DeFi (same family, different book)

Ethereum DeFi and BSC DeFi are the same **family of programs**: routers, pools, ERC-20-style tokens, approvals, gas paid in a native coin. They are not the same **book**. Intermediate already failed people who treated chain ID 1 and chain ID 56 as nicknames.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to compare the two books on the facts that bite a DeFi user: chain ID, native fuel, explorer, token standard name, and where Crystal Stones actually lives. This academy will not tell you to buy ETH or BNB.

## Same family

Both chains run EVM-style contracts. That is why the same wallet apps can add both networks. That is why a swap on BSC feels like a swap on Ethereum: approve, then call a router, then a pool inventory changes. **BEP-20** is BSC’s name for the ERC-20-style interface. Allowance, `transferFrom`, decimals — the same debit-order design.

Copied: address shape, transaction shape, ABI idea, “Contract Interaction” in the wallet, the habit of reading an explorer. Not copied: state, validator set, the list of deployed contracts, the native coin, the explorer’s database, the gas price in local units.

A USDT row on Ethereum is a row in Ethereum’s USDT contract. A USDT row on BSC is a row in BSC’s USDT contract. Same letters on the bottle. Different notebooks. A pool that holds “USDT/WETH” on Ethereum does not hold your BSC USDT.

## Different book

**Ethereum mainnet:** chain ID **1**, native coin **ETH**, explorer **Etherscan**. **BNB Smart Chain:** chain ID **56**, native coin **BNB**, explorer **BscScan**. Cheap gas on BSC is why this academy can ask for tiny practice without turning every test into a painful fee. Cheap gas is also why copycat tokens and copycat routers breed. Attackers like cheap books too.

Dear gas on Ethereum does not make a router honest. A verified scam on Etherscan is still a scam. “I paid a lot” is not an audit.

TABLE
Fact | Ethereum DeFi | BSC DeFi
Chain ID | 1 | 56
Fuel for every call | ETH | BNB
Public window | Etherscan | BscScan
Token interface style | ERC-20 (and others) | BEP-20 (ERC-20-style)
Where Crystal Stones is published | Not the home this academy verifies | BEP-20 `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`, verify only
Same-looking 0x | A name on this book | A name on that book — not a bridge
ENDTABLE

## Bridged is not the same as native, and neither is a blessing

People wrap, bridge, and rename. A wrapped native coin (WETH, WBNB) is a token program that represents the native coin inside ERC-20-style plumbing so pools can hold it. A bridged asset is a claim program on the destination chain. Those are extra contracts and extra failure cases. This course will not teach you to bridge as a skill. It will tell you to **name which contract you actually hold** before you approve a router.

Crystal Stones on BSC is the published BEP-20 this academy points at for verification. A ticker that says Crystal Stones on Ethereum is a different object until proven otherwise. Do not send the BEP-20 token to an Ethereum pool because a website used the same word.

**Worked scenario.** A learner wants to practice a tiny swap “like the tutorial screenshot.”

1. The learner reads the screenshot’s network badge — or notices it has none, which is already a problem.
2. The learner sets the wallet to one chain and one chain only: 56 with BNB, or 1 with ETH.
3. The learner opens the matching explorer from a bookmark and pastes the router hex from a source that is not the first search ad.
4. The learner checks the token contracts the pool claims to hold, not the ticker letters on the website.
5. The learner does not try the other chain “because the address looks the same.”

DIAGRAM
WALLET SCREEN (looks identical)
[ Ethereum  chain 1 ]              [ BSC  chain 56 ]
[ Router 0xAbc...   ]              [ Router 0xAbc... ]
[ Pool USDT / WETH  ]              [ Pool USDT / WBNB ]
[ Fuel: ETH         ]              [ Fuel: BNB         ]
         \                                /
          \                              /
           v                            v
     Etherscan history            BscScan history
     (inventory A)                (inventory B)
ENDDIAGRAM

## Binance is still not BNB Smart Chain

Binance the company is an example of a centralised exchange. BNB Smart Chain is a public book. BNB the coin is fuel on that book and also an asset on the exchange. Withdrawing “USDT” from an exchange is a multiple-choice question about networks. Pick the book your wallet and your DeFi program actually use. The help desk cannot unwrite a public page if you chose the other book.

Academy checkout for this Intermediate course is **$10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout**. That is BSC’s USDT, not Ethereum’s USDT, and not Crystal Stones token.

NOTE
Academy rule: name four things before you approve a DeFi spender — asset contract, chain ID, explorer, fuel coin. If any of the four is guessed, stop. Same family is not same book.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You will stop saying “DeFi” as if it were one computer. Next: the list of things this course will refuse, including yield shopping.

## Say this out loud

- Ethereum DeFi and BSC DeFi are the same family of programs on two books.
- Chain ID 1 burns ETH. Chain ID 56 burns BNB. State is not shared.
- BEP-20 is ERC-20-style plumbing, not a second physics.
- Crystal Stones is verified as a BEP-20 on BSC, not as a pool on Ethereum.
- Cheap gas is not an honesty stamp; dear gas is not one either.

Next: what this course will not teach — including why we will not shop for yield.

lessons.title: What this course will not teach (no yield shopping)
lessons.content:
# What this course will not teach (no yield shopping)

Intermediate is where academies get greedy. They start ranking farms, reprinting APY screenshots, and calling that “DeFi education.” This course will not. It will teach the objects — router, pool, allowance, collateral, LP receipt — so a percentage has fewer places to hide.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to tell a friend what six modules buy them, what they still will not be, and how this $10 track is actually paid for. This academy will not tell you to buy Crystal Stones, ETH, BNB, or a pool share.

## What you should be able to do by the last quiz

After six modules you should be able to: explain DeFi as programs that claim swap, pool, and lend; split an app from a protocol; read an allowance on an explorer and revoke it without folklore; describe a pool as inventories, not as a magic price machine; describe supplying as protocol custody with a liquidation function; describe an LP token as a receipt; and name the failure cases that empty wallets — fake frontends, unlimited approvals, wrong chain, and rugs that are functions.

You should **not** expect to be a quant, a farmer, an auditor, a liquidation bot operator, or a recovery agent. You should not expect a list of “safe” protocols. Safe is not a sticker this academy prints.

## Yield shopping is a different course, and not this one

**Yield** is a word ads use for “this program promises extra tokens if you lock or stake.” Sometimes the extra is swap fees. Sometimes it is a newly minted reward token. Sometimes it is a screenshot. Shopping for the largest percentage trains you to skip liquidation, skip allowance, and skip the admin key.

This course will mention fees and reward programs only as objects that exist, so you can see the extra contract on top. It will not compare APYs. It will not invent a Crystal Stones farm. Crystal Stones’ mineral-vault story remains **their claim to verify**, not a yield product.

TABLE
You might want | This course gives | This course refuses
A high APY list | Why a percentage can hide liquidation and admin mint | A ranking, a “best farm,” a telegram tip
A job in DeFi | Vocabulary and failure cases | A placement or a salary
A way to pay Intermediate | $10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout | Crystal Stones token, ETH, a chat-paste 0x
An audit of a pool | How to name router, pool, allowance, explorer | A certificate that the pool is safe
Trading skill | Slippage and sandwich as pictures of how the design hurts | Entries, leverage, signals
ENDTABLE

## How the $10 actually works

This course is **paid Intermediate**. Price is **$10 USDT on BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20)** through **academy checkout** or a third-party payment processor. That sentence is complete. It does not include ETH. It does not include the Crystal Stones token. It does not include a personal wallet an instructor pasted in chat.

The Crystal Stones contract `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` is listed so you can **verify** the published BEP-20 asset. Verification is not payment. If a checkout page ever tells you to send Crystal Stones to that contract, the page is wrong or hostile. Academy staff will never ask for a seed phrase, a private key, or 2FA codes to “unlock Module 2.”

Practice, when we ask for it, is tiny amounts you can lose. Prefer a test-size approve and a test-size swap on a named chain. Testnet — a practice computer with worthless play coins — is a valid drill. Rent money is not.

**Worked scenario.** A learner finished the Ethereum Intermediate course and wants this DeFi course.

1. The learner checks the course card: level intermediate, price $10, paid track.
2. The learner looks for academy checkout in USDT BEP-20, not a direct message.
3. The learner ignores a “support” account that says pay in Crystal Stones for a discount.
4. The learner does not approve a router in order to pay tuition. Tuition is not a swap.
5. The learner starts Module 2 knowing this classroom is a seeing course, not a farm tour.

DIAGRAM
PAYING FOR THIS COURSE                 NOT PAYING FOR THIS COURSE
+---------------------------+          +---------------------------+
| Learner                   |          | Learner                   |
| $10 USDT BEP-20           |          | Crystal Stones token      |
+-------------+-------------+          | ETH on Ethereum           |
              |                        | seed phrase to "support"  |
              v                        +-------------+-------------+
+---------------------------+                        |
| academy checkout /        |                        v
| third-party processor     |          hostile or simply the wrong object
+---------------------------+
ENDDIAGRAM

## The voice you should expect

Global. Adult. You plus the object: wallet, router, pool, explorer, invoice. Worked scenarios are numbered technical walkthroughs, not a cast. When Trust Wallet or MetaMask appears, they are examples of wallet apps. When Binance appears, it is an example of a centralised exchange. If a lesson feels like a rally, it has failed. If a lesson feels like a glossary dump, it has failed.

NOTE
Academy rule: you are not behind if you still look up chain ID 56. You are behind if you sign an unlimited approve because a percentage was large. Use this course as a brake, not as a dare.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

This is the map and the ethics in one place, so later modules can go faster without smuggling a shop. Next module: approvals, routers, and how a token actually leaves your row.

## Say this out loud

- This course teaches DeFi as programs and as failure cases, not as yield shopping.
- It does not rank farms, give buy orders, or staff a recovery desk.

- Crystal Stones’ contract is verify-only, never a payment address.

lessons.title: Approve is a debit order (reuse Ethereum, go deeper)
lessons.content:
# Approve is a debit order (reuse Ethereum, go deeper)

The Ethereum course already named **approve**: a storage write on a token program that sets how many units a **spender** may pull from your row with `transferFrom`. This lesson takes that object into DeFi, where almost every swap and deposit starts with the same debit order, often set to a number so large it might as well be forever.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say what an approval is, why a DeFi button asks for it, and why “I signed once” is not the same sentence as “I swapped once.” This academy will not tell you to approve any router.

## The token program is the bank clerk

USDT, WBNB, Crystal Stones as a BEP-20, any ERC-20-style token — the list of balances lives in the token contract. Your wallet shows a number. The number is not coins in the wallet app. The number is a row. To let a router move that row, the token program must be told: this spender may take up to this amount.

**Approve** is that instruction. It is not a send. After approve, your visible balance can stay the same. What changed is **allowance** — a second number, keyed by (you, spender). The Ethereum picture was a standing debit order. Keep it. DeFi is where people sign the debit order with the word unlimited and then are surprised months later.

A **spender** is usually another contract: a router, a lending pool, a “zap,” an aggregator. It is not the website. If the website is cloned, the spender hex in the wallet pop is the object that matters.

## Unlimited is a convenience with a memory

Many frontends ask for the maximum uint256 value so they never have to ask again. That is convenient. It is also a debit order that survives the swap, survives disconnecting the site, and survives you forgetting the site existed. If the spender is later hacked, or if it was hostile from the first minute, it can pull until the allowance is spent or revoked. Your later deposits refill the same drain.

Exact-amount approve is slower UX: you sign approve, then you sign the swap, and next week you sign approve again. Slower is not morally better in every case. It is a smaller standing order. This course will not pretend one button is always right. It will refuse the folklore that unlimited is “just how DeFi works, so it is safe.”

TABLE
Action | What storage changes | What your wallet shows next | What can still happen later
Approve 50 USDT to a router | Allowance(you, router) = 50 | Balance unchanged | Router may pull up to 50
Approve unlimited | Allowance = a huge number | Balance unchanged | Router may pull until you revoke or you are empty
Swap after approve | Token rows move; allowance may decrease | Token A down, token B up | If allowance remains, another pull is still legal
Disconnect the website | Nothing on-chain | Site gone from the session list | Allowance remains
ENDTABLE

## Approve is a separate transaction from the job

On most EVM designs you pay gas twice for a first-time swap: once to write allowance, once to call the router. Both burn native coin — ETH on chain 1, BNB on chain 56. A failed approve still costs gas if the transaction was mined and reverted or if you set a fee and it landed. The Ethereum course taught “failed still costs.” DeFi does not repeal that.

Some newer token designs use `permit` (a signature that sets allowance without a separate on-chain approve). That is still a debit order. It is just packed differently. If a wallet asks you to sign typed data you do not understand, treat it as an approval request and read the spender.

Crystal Stones is a BEP-20. It can have allowances like any other. The published contract `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` is verify-only. Do not approve a mystery spender because a page said “official CS DeFi.” Do not pay this course by approving anyone. Tuition is **$10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout**.

**Worked scenario.** A learner taps Swap. The wallet pops Approve.

1. The learner reads the network: chain 56 needs BNB; chain 1 needs ETH.
2. The learner reads the token and the spender hex, not only the website title.
3. The learner notices whether the amount is a small number or the word unlimited (or a string of 1s and Fs).
4. The learner compares the spender to a router address on the explorer from a bookmark.
5. If the spender is unknown, the learner rejects. If the learner proceeds at all, the size is a practice amount they can lose.

DIAGRAM
BEFORE APPROVE                     AFTER APPROVE (NO SWAP YET)
+----------------------+           +----------------------+
| Token program        |           | Token program        |
| balance(you) = 100   |           | balance(you) = 100   |
| allowance(you, R) = 0|           | allowance(you, R) = UNLIMITED
+----------------------+           +----------------------+
Wallet still shows 100. The debit order is already live.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Staff will not ask you to approve “the academy”

Academy staff will never send a spender hex in chat “to unlock the module.” They will never ask for a seed, a private key, or 2FA. A debit order is something you create, on a chain you named, for a program you looked up.

NOTE
Academy rule: approve is not a handshake with a brand. It is a number in a token program that says a spender may pull. Read the spender. Prefer small practice sizes. Unlimited is a memory, not a courtesy.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You reused the Ethereum debit-order picture and planted it in DeFi, where the first button is often the dangerous one. Next: the usual spender — the router.

## Say this out loud

- Approve writes allowance; it does not send tokens by itself.
- Unlimited approve is a standing debit order that survives the swap and the disconnect.
- The spender is a contract hex, not a website title.
- Gas for approve is native coin on that chain, separate from the later swap.
- This academy will not ask you to approve a router to pay tuition.

Next: router contracts — the program that talks to pools on your behalf.

lessons.title: Router contracts
lessons.content:
# Router contracts

A **router** is a program that takes a user’s swap (or add/remove liquidity) and calls one or more **pools**. You almost never tap the pool first. You tap a button. The button asks your wallet to call the router. If you approved the router, it can pull the input token and send you the output token.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say what a router is for, why so many DeFi screens hide it, and why approving “the exchange” is really approving this contract. This academy will not tell you which router to use.

## Why a router exists

A pool holds two inventories and a pricing rule. A useful swap might need a path: token A to token B through token C, across two pools. The router’s job is to walk that path in one transaction so you do not have to hold the middle token or sign twice. It is plumbing. It is also a **spender** with a wide job: many tokens, many pools, many functions.

Routers usually have functions with names like `swapExactTokensForTokens`, `addLiquidity`, `removeLiquidity`. You do not need to memorise the list. You need to know that **the router is allowed to pull whatever you approved**, then call pools, then send leftovers to an address in the call data — hopefully yours.

A **factory** is a related program that creates pool contracts. You rarely approve the factory for a simple swap. You meet it when a new pair is first created. Do not confuse factory, router, and pool. Three programs. Three addresses. One website drawing all three as a single logo.

## The router is the debit-order counterparty

When a frontend says “allow USDT to trade,” the spender is typically the router, not the pool, not the company, not academy checkout. If you later use a different website that talks to the **same** router, your old allowance still applies. If you use a website that talks to a **different** router, you are looking at a new spender and a new debit order.

Copycat routers are a standard attack. They speak enough of the same ABI that a wallet shows a familiar function name. They take the pulled tokens and do not send the output you expected. The explorer will show a successful transaction. Success means the call did not revert. It does not mean you got a fair swap.

TABLE
Object | Typical job | You approve it? | Failure if you mix it up
Pool | Holds inventories; prices a swap against x*y=k (Module 3) | Rarely, for some designs | Sending tokens straight to a pool with no call
Router | Paths your call through pools | Usually yes | Unlimited approve to a copycat router
Factory | Creates new pool contracts | Rarely for a swap | Treating a create-pair event as “the exchange”
Frontend | Draws buttons | Never — it is not a chain object | Thinking the domain is the spender
ENDTABLE

## Path, recipient, and deadline are not decorations

A router call usually names: which tokens, how much in, minimum out, the path of pool hops, the **recipient** address, and a **deadline**. If the recipient is not your EOA, the output goes elsewhere. If the deadline is already past, the call should revert — and you still pay gas for the attempt. If the path uses a pool you did not inspect, you are swapping against an inventory you did not name.

Wallet apps such as Trust Wallet and MetaMask — examples only — may show a decoded function if they know the ABI. If they show only “Contract Interaction,” you are signing a blind call. Blind calls are how routers get replaced under a familiar logo.

Crystal Stones as a BEP-20 can appear in a path if a pool exists. That is not a reason to buy it, and not a reason to treat the published verify-only hex as a router. Tuition remains **$10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout**.

**Worked scenario.** A learner is asked to “use the official router.”

1. The learner opens the explorer for the correct chain from a bookmark.
2. The learner pastes the router hex and checks it is a contract with verified-or-at-least-present bytecode, not an EOA.
3. The learner looks at recent transactions: do they look like swaps, or like a newly born drain?
4. The learner checks the approve spender in the wallet against that same hex.
5. The learner uses a tiny input size. A router that works for 1 USDT can still be the wrong object for a life-changing amount, and this academy will not name a life-changing amount.

DIAGRAM
YOUR CALL                         WHERE IT GOES
+------------------+              +------------------+
| EOA signs        |              | Router           |
| to: 0xROUTER     | ------------>| pulls token A    |
| fn: swap...      |              | calls pool 1     |
+------------------+              | maybe pool 2     |
                                  | sends token B    |
                                  +--------+---------+
                                           |
                                           v
                                  +------------------+
                                  | recipient (hope  |
                                  | this is your EOA)|
                                  +------------------+
ENDDIAGRAM

## A router does not owe you a help desk

If the call succeeds and the recipient was wrong, the book will not parent you. If the call reverts, you lost gas, not (usually) the input token. If the router has an admin upgrade, yesterday’s bytecode is not today’s. Module 6 treats upgradeable hostility. Today: name the router as a program with a hex, not as a brand.

NOTE
Academy rule: you approve a router hex on a named chain. You do not approve “DeFi,” “the exchange,” or “Crystal Stones support.” If a chat sends a router address, it is not this academy.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can now point at the router as the usual spender that talks to pools. Next: allowance and balance as two different numbers, so a zero screen does not mean a dead debit order.

## Say this out loud

- A router is a program that paths a swap or liquidity call through pools.
- Factory, router, and pool are three addresses; a website is a fourth, off-chain object.
- Approving “the exchange” is usually approving the router hex.
- Recipient and path in the call matter as much as the button label.
- A successful router transaction means “did not revert,” not “this was fair.”

Next: allowance versus balance — the two numbers that DeFi wallets love to flatten.

lessons.title: Allowance vs balance
lessons.content:
# Allowance vs balance

**Balance** is how many units the token program says your address owns. **Allowance** is how many units it will let a given spender pull. Wallets shout the first number. DeFi risk lives in the second. If you only watch balance, you will think you are safe when you are empty and still wide open when you refill.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to hold both numbers at once, including the ugly case: balance 0, allowance unlimited. This academy will not tell you to keep either number large.

## Two keys in the same notebook

Inside an ERC-20-style contract, storage has a map of balances and a map of allowances. `balanceOf(you)` is one read. `allowance(you, spender)` is another. A swap that uses `transferFrom` checks the allowance, pulls up to that cap, and (in the standard design) decreases the allowance unless it was the infinite value some implementations treat as sticky.

Your wallet app may not show allowance at all. Trust Wallet and MetaMask — examples of wallet apps — often show token lists and dollar-named totals. They may hide spender permissions behind a settings screen or leave them to an explorer. The number you glance at is not the debit order.

If a spender is allowed 1,000 USDT and you hold 40, it can take 40. If you later receive 900, it can take more, until the remaining allowance is exhausted — or forever, if you signed unlimited.

## Zero balance is not a closed debit order

People “clean out” a wallet, see 0, and screenshot safety. The allowance row can still be a huge number. The next inbound transfer — a payroll, a refund, a test send from a friend — is then pullable. Attackers sometimes wait. They sometimes leave a dust balance so you do not abandon the address.

Revoke is the tool that sets allowance toward zero. The next lesson reads it; the one after that revokes it. Today you only need the split: **empty is not revoked.**

TABLE
What you see | Balance | Allowance to router R | What R may pull now
“I have 200 USDT” | 200 | 0 | Nothing via transferFrom
“I swapped once, still 80” | 80 | unlimited | Up to 80 now, and more if you refill
“I sent it all away” | 0 | unlimited | Nothing now; everything that arrives later
“I revoked” | 80 | 0 | Nothing via that spender until you approve again
ENDTABLE

## Native coin has no ERC-20 allowance

ETH on Ethereum and BNB on BSC are native balances on the account, not rows in a token program. A router call that spends native coin uses `value` on the transaction, not `approve`. Wrapped native (WETH, WBNB) is a token program: it does use allowance. Mixing those two is how people “approve BNB” in their head and then sign an unlimited WBNB approve with their hand.

Gas is always native. You can have a large token balance, a large allowance, and still be stuck because you cannot pay the router call. You can also have a tiny native balance, tap a revoke, and fail because revoke costs gas too.

Crystal Stones, as a BEP-20, has balance and allowance like USDT. Seeing a Crystal Stones row does not mean you approved a spender, and approving a spender does not pay academy tuition. Checkout is **$10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout**. The published CS hex is verify-only.

**Worked scenario.** A learner’s wallet shows 0 USDT after a swap.

1. The learner does not celebrate. The learner names the router they approved an hour ago.
2. The learner will, in the next lesson, read `allowance(learner, router)` on the explorer.
3. The learner does not send a fresh USDT paycheck to that EOA until they know the allowance number.
4. The learner checks they still have native coin — not because USDT pays gas, but because the next action needs fuel.
5. The learner ignores a chat that says “send Crystal Stones to reset allowance.” Allowance is a token-program write, not a tribute.

DIAGRAM
TOKEN PROGRAM STORAGE (same contract)
+---------------------------+     +---------------------------+
| balances                  |     | allowances                |
| you -> 0 USDT             |     | you, router -> UNLIMITED  |
| pool -> 50,000 USDT       |     | you, other -> 0           |
+---------------------------+     +---------------------------+
LEFT is the screenshot. RIGHT is the debit order. They are not twins.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Aggregators multiply the spender list

Some apps route through an aggregator contract that then calls several routers. You may approve the aggregator, not the famous router you thought you were using. Each extra spender is an extra debit order to track. This course will not rank aggregators. It will tell you to read the spender hex every time the wallet pops.

NOTE
Academy rule: quote two numbers before you call a wallet “empty” — native fuel, and allowance for each spender you remember. If you cannot name the spenders, you are not done. You are guessing.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can now refuse the single-number screenshot. Next: how to actually read allowance on Etherscan or BscScan without a folklore app.

## Say this out loud

- Balance is what you own in the token list; allowance is what a spender may pull.
- Zero balance with unlimited allowance is an open debit order waiting for a refill.
- Native ETH or BNB does not use ERC-20 approve; wrapped versions do.
- An aggregator is another spender, not a synonym for the famous router.
- Crystal Stones balance is not tuition; checkout is USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout.

Next: reading allowance on an explorer — a Read Contract call, not a vibe.

lessons.title: How to read allowance on an explorer
lessons.content:
# How to read allowance on an explorer

Allowance is a public number. You do not need a branded “revoke app” to see it. You need the token contract, your address, the spender address, and the explorer for that chain. The Ethereum course already taught Read Contract. This lesson uses that tab for the debit order.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to walk a Read Contract query for `allowance(owner, spender)` on BscScan or Etherscan and interpret zero, a small number, and a wall of f’s. This academy will not tell you to connect a third-party “approval checker” as a requirement.

## Gather four objects first

**1. Chain.** Chain ID 1 → Etherscan. Chain ID 56 → BscScan. Open it from a bookmark. A fake explorer will happily show a fake zero.

**2. Token contract.** Not the ticker. USDT on BSC is not USDT on Ethereum. Crystal Stones, if you are verifying the published asset, is `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on BSC — verify only, not a spender, not checkout.

**3. Owner.** Your EOA. The address the wallet app shows for that network.

**4. Spender.** The router or aggregator you approved. If you do not have this hex, you cannot finish the read. You may find it in a previous transaction: look for an `Approval` event on the token’s page, or for the `to` address of your approve transaction.

Some explorers offer an “Approval Checker” or token-approval list. Those are convenience views of the same events. They are not magic. They can be incomplete if you used a different token or a different chain. The raw Read Contract call is the skill.

## Read Contract is a view, not a send

On the token’s explorer page, open **Contract** → **Read**. Find `allowance`. Paste owner, then spender. The returned integer is the remaining debit order, in the token’s smallest units. You must know **decimals**. USDT is often 18 on BSC and 6 on Ethereum — do not assume. Divide by 10^decimals to get the human amount. A value that looks like 2^256-1 (a long string of 9s, or 0xfff…) is unlimited for practical purposes.

Calling Read Contract does not cost gas. It does not require connecting a wallet. If a page demands a wallet connection only to *display* allowance, you are in an app layer. You may refuse and use the explorer’s read tab instead.

TABLE
Returned value | Practical meaning | Next move
0 | That spender cannot transferFrom right now | No revoke needed for this pair
A modest integer | Remaining cap | Decide if you still want that cap
A huge integer / max uint | Unlimited standing order | Treat as open until you revoke
Error / empty | Wrong chain, wrong contract, or not a token | Stop guessing; check the four objects
ENDTABLE

## Approval events are a paper trail

Token programs emit an **Approval** event when allowance is written. On the token’s explorer page, the Events tab can show owner, spender, and value. A later approve of zero should emit a matching event. Events are history. The Read call is the current number. Use both if they disagree: the current number wins for what the spender can do *now*.

Wallet apps may also list “connected sites.” That list is sessions, not allowances. You already killed that confusion in Module 1. Do not use the connected-site list as an allowance report.

**Worked scenario.** A learner wants to know whether a router can still pull USDT on BSC.

1. The learner opens BscScan from a bookmark (chain 56).
2. The learner pastes the USDT BEP-20 contract they actually hold — not a screenshot ticker, not Crystal Stones’ verify-only hex unless they are reading CS allowance on purpose.
3. The learner opens Read Contract → `allowance`, pastes their EOA as owner and the router as spender.
4. The learner notes decimals and converts the integer, or recognises the unlimited pattern.
5. The learner does not send USDT, BNB, or Crystal Stones to the explorer, to the token contract, or to a chat that offered to “check approvals for a fee.”

DIAGRAM
EXPLORER READ (view only)              WALLET POP (would cost gas)
+---------------------------+          +---------------------------+
| Token contract page       |          | Approve / write           |
| Read: allowance(you, R)   |          | changes storage           |
| result: integer           |          | burns native coin         |
+---------------------------+          +---------------------------+
LEFT is looking. RIGHT is changing. Do not confuse the tabs.
ENDDIAGRAM

## What this academy will not make you install

You do not need a new app to read a number. You do not need to paste a seed into an “approval dashboard.” Staff will never ask for a seed, a private key, or 2FA to “pull your allowance report.” Tuition is not an approval check. Tuition is **$10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout**.

NOTE
Academy rule: four objects — chain, token contract, owner, spender — then one read. If a helper site wants a signature only to show you a number, you already have a better tool: the explorer’s Read tab.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can now fetch the debit-order number without folklore. Next: revoke as approve-zero, without rituals.

## Say this out loud

- Allowance is a public read: owner, spender, token contract, named chain.
- Read Contract does not cost gas and does not require connecting a wallet.
- A max-uint result is an unlimited standing order, not a decoration.
- Approval events are history; the read is the current cap.
- Connected sites in a wallet are not an allowance report.

Next: revoke without folklore — set the number to zero, pay gas, and know what that does not undo.

lessons.title: Revoke without folklore
lessons.content:
# Revoke without folklore

**Revoke** means: write allowance for that spender back to zero (or to a smaller number). On ERC-20-style tokens, that write is usually another `approve`, this time with amount 0. It is not a spell. It does not reverse a pull that already happened. It does not recover tokens. It does not need a special “official revoke chain.”

By the end of this lesson you should be able to describe a revoke as a paid storage write, list what it cannot repair, and refuse apps that ask for a seed to “clear permissions.” This academy will not tell you which helper website to use.

## Revoke is approve(spender, 0)

The token program already has the function. You call it. You pay gas in the native coin of that chain. After the transaction succeeds, `allowance(you, spender)` should read 0. If it does not, you are on the wrong chain, the wrong token, or the transaction never wrote what you thought.

Some tokens have a non-standard approve (they require you to set zero before a new non-zero amount). That quirk can make a revoke-and-reapprove dance. It is still the same object: a number in storage. Helper sites that batch many revokes are calling the same functions and charging you gas per write, plus whatever extra their own contract does. Read the spender they are asking you to call.

A revoke does not move your balance. If a hostile spender already pulled, those units are in someone else’s row. The Ethereum safety habit still applies: tiny practice sizes so a pull is not a life.

## What revoke will not do

It will not stop a transaction that is already in the mempool. It will not cancel a swap that already succeeded. It will not close a lending position. It will not burn an LP token. It will not unsandwich you. It will not parent a wrong-chain send. It will not pay or refund academy checkout.

It will not replace self-custody hygiene. If someone has your private key, they can approve again after you revoke. Revoke is for the case where **you still hold the key** and a spender still holds a debit order.

TABLE
Action | Changes allowance? | Returns stolen tokens? | Costs gas?
Revoke (approve 0) | Yes, toward zero | No | Yes, native coin
Disconnect website | No | No | No
Hide the token in the wallet UI | No | No | No
Send remaining balance to a new EOA | No (old EOA still has the allowance) | No — it just moves what is left | Yes
Give staff your seed “to revoke for you” | That is theft | No | You lose the account
ENDTABLE

## New address versus revoke

Moving to a new EOA leaves the old allowance on the old address. That is useful if the old key might be copied. It is not a revoke. The old address’s remaining tokens are still pullable until you move them **and** you accept that any later send to the old address is at risk. A new address also needs its own native coin for gas. Do not send the seed of the old address to the new app. Importing a seed is the same key.

Crystal Stones revoke would be an approve-zero on the BEP-20 token, if you ever approved a spender for it. That is not a payment. Do not send CS to `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` “to clear.” That contract is verify-only. Do not send USDT there either. Course payment is **$10 USDT BEP-20 through academy checkout**.

**Worked scenario.** A learner found an unlimited allowance to a router they no longer want.

1. The learner confirms chain, token, owner, spender on the explorer Read tab.
2. The learner checks native coin for gas — BNB on 56, ETH on 1.
3. The learner calls approve(spender, 0) from the wallet or the explorer’s Write tab, having verified they are on the real explorer.
4. The learner waits for the transaction to succeed, then reads allowance again. The second read is the proof, not the wallet’s happy toast.
5. The learner does not paste a seed into a “one-click revoke all chains” page.

DIAGRAM
BEFORE REVOKE                      AFTER SUCCESSFUL REVOKE
+----------------------+           +----------------------+
| allowance(you, R)    |           | allowance(you, R)    |
| = UNLIMITED          |           | = 0                  |
| balance = 80         |           | balance = 80         |

Same balance. Dead debit order. Stolen units, if any, are not in this picture.

## Folklore to drop

“Revoke on a full moon.” No. “Revoke only with this sponsored tool.” No. “Revoke by sending 0 tokens to yourself.” No. “Academy support can revoke if you share 2FA.” No. Staff will never ask for seed, key, or 2FA. A revoke is your signed write, on a named token, on a named chain.

NOTE
Academy rule: revoke is a paid, boring write. Proof is a post-transaction allowance read of zero. Anything that wants a seed to do this job is not a revoke tool.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You can now retire a debit order without a ritual. Next module: the pools those routers actually talk to — inventories, not slogans.

## Say this out loud

- Revoke is approve(spender, 0), a storage write that costs native gas.
- It does not reverse a pull that already succeeded.
- Disconnecting a site is not revoke; hiding a token is not revoke.
- A new EOA does not erase the old address’s allowances.
- Academy staff will never ask for a seed to “clear approvals.”

Next: a pool is two (or more) inventories in a program — the object a router calls.
